title: The Lovers of the Banu Ozrah

keywords: the lovers of the banu ozrah
full_text:
Among the ancient tribes of Arabia, none was more renowned for the purity of their affection and the delicacy of their verses than the noble clan of Banu Ozrah. It was proverbial throughout the desert that when a youth of the Banu Ozrah loved, he loved with his whole soul, and if parted, his spirit would pine away in steadfast fidelity rather than compromise with fickle sentiment.

An elder traveler of Baghdad, journeying through the fertile valleys of the Hijaz, pitched his tent near a Bedouin encampment. At eventide, as the campfires flickered against the crimson dunes, he heard a young shepherd reciting verses of sublime beauty beside an ancient spring.

The youth sang of a maiden named Lubna, whose eyes were like the gazelles of the morning and whose character was purer than desert rain. When the traveler approached, the youth welcomed him with customary desert hospitality, sharing his bowl of fresh camel’s milk and dates.

'Why do you weep into the spring, young brother?' asked the traveler.

The youth sighed: 'Lubna and I were betrothed from our childhood, our hearts knit together by shared poetry and honor. But her kinsmen, demanding a great herd of red camels which my poor father does not possess, have decreed that she must be given to an affluent chieftain of the north. We have sworn an oath: though our bodies be separated by hundreds of leagues of sand, our hearts shall remain as pure and faithful as the stars that never wander from their course.'

Moved to tears by their noble devotion, the generous traveler rode immediately to the camp of Lubna’s father. He opened his leather pouches, weighed out fifty gold dinars, and purchased fifty fine red camels from the caravans of Mecca, presenting them to the bride’s father on the youth’s behalf.

The clan celebrated the union of Lubna and her faithful poet with ten days of joyous festivities, and the traveler departed with a peaceful heart, knowing that he had preserved the most sacred virtue of the Banu Ozrah.
moral: Pure love founded on spiritual nobility, chastity, and devotion transcends all earthly sorrow.
